neighbours.label: Economics prose about how growth or policy affects welfare and distribution (living standards, wages, inequality, the poor), as opposed to market efficiency or prices
fire: Decades of trade liberalisation have done little to lift living standards for families in the poorest regions.
Critics say the austerity programme hurt wages and pushed more pensioners into poverty.
A bloated banking sector can be harmful for an economy, because it deepens the divide between the wealthy and everyone else.
Without public investment in schools and health, growth will not reduce inequality or improve the lives of the poor.
The report finds that the boom raised incomes at the top while ordinary workers saw their pay stagnate.
Many development economists now believe that widening inequality holds back growth and harms the middle class.
Higher minimum wages and stronger safety nets would improve living standards for low-paid workers, the study argues.
The recession damaged household incomes most severely among the young and the unskilled.
quiet: Decades of trade liberalisation have made bond markets more liquid and narrowed the spread between bid and offer prices.
Traders say the new auction system lets prices adjust to fresh information within seconds.
A crowded gym can be harmful for an athlete, because it shortens the time available on each machine.
Without regular investment in tracks and signals, trains will not run on time or reach the coast before dark.
The report finds that the storm raised water levels at the dam while smaller streams saw their flow slow down.
Many arbitrage desks now believe that futures contracts are priced efficiently relative to the underlying index.
Higher safety standards and stronger helmets would improve results for junior riders, the coach argues.
The frost damaged vineyard crops most severely among the young vines and the late varieties.
